title: The medium is the message: How neurometabolic entanglement generates conscious experience
summary: Most neuroscientific accounts of consciousness assume that conscious experience is constituted by the information conveyed between neurons. The physical-chemical details of the metabolic and physiological processes that convey this information are correspondingly presumed to be relevant only insofar as they support the organization of information processes. We describe an alternative perspective that denies this presumed independence of the processing of neural information and the metabolic-physiological details of these processes. We call this alternative paradigm the theory of neuro-metabolic entanglement (NME). NME proposes that mental experience exemplifies the inseparability of the organization of neural information processes from the constraints imposed by the material-energetic properties of the neural medium itself. Central to this account is a recursive, Möbius-like loop of neural connections that entangles patterns of forebrain information processing with midbrain regulatory systems that modulate forebrain metabolism. This enables patterns of neural activity to indirectly modify the global distribution of metabolic resources underlying these information processes. It also constitutes a bottleneck that integrates diverse neural processes into an adaptively relevant unitary experience organized in terms of the global redistribution of metabolic support. Computational models of neural function cannot treat energy supply as a fixed background parameter; our proposed Möbius-like loop of neuro-metabolic entanglement offers a framework for future models in which neural activity is dynamically and recursively modulated by the network's own metabolism. Recognizing this entanglement is a first step toward dissolving the explanatory gap highlighted by the so-called "hard problem" of consciousness.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the "theory of neuro-metabolic entanglement" (NME), arguing that conscious experience cannot be reduced to information processing alone but arises from an inseparable, recursive entanglement of neural information organization with the metabolic/energetic constraints of the neural medium, mediated by a Möbius-like loop linking forebrain processing to midbrain metabolic regulation.
AI.motivation: Most neuroscientific accounts assume consciousness is constituted by information conveyed between neurons, treating metabolic and physiological details as merely supportive background. The authors challenge this presumed independence of information processing from the material-energetic substrate, aiming to address the explanatory gap of the "hard problem" of consciousness.
AI.method: Conceptual/theoretical framework construction. The authors articulate NME as an alternative paradigm, positing a recursive, Möbius-like loop of neural connections that entangles forebrain information-processing patterns with midbrain regulatory systems modulating forebrain metabolism—forming a bottleneck that integrates diverse processes into a unitary, adaptively relevant experience. They also argue computational models should treat energy supply as dynamically coupled rather than a fixed parameter.
AI.result: The proposed Möbius-like loop allows neural activity to indirectly modify the global distribution of metabolic resources underlying information processes, integrating diverse neural processes into a unitary experience organized by global metabolic redistribution. The framework implies that energy supply cannot be treated as a fixed background parameter in computational models.
AI.conclusion: Recognizing neuro-metabolic entanglement is presented as a first step toward dissolving the explanatory gap highlighted by the hard problem of consciousness, offering a framework for future models in which neural activity is dynamically and recursively modulated by the network's own metabolism.

title: Gate-Based Feature Importance in Simulation-Based Inference for EEG: A Cautionary Tale
comment: Accepted (non-archival) at NeurIPS 2026 workshops Sim2Science and Interp4Discovery. Code: https://github.com/Shrivatsa-Deshmukh/sbi-gate-vs-ablation
summary: Simulation-based inference (SBI) provides a powerful way to fit mechanistic models to data, but offers little insight into which information in the data shapes the inferred parameter values. It could therefore benefit from robust and inexpensive interpretability methods. Learned weighting mechanisms such as feature gates provide a potential route to low-cost interpretability, although their interpretation assumes that predictive training reveals which inputs drive performance. We examined this assumption in a computational neuroscience setting, where neural posterior estimation (NPE) is used to infer four physiological parameters of a dynamical model of interacting neuronal populations (Jansen-Rit). We tested whether the learned gate weights captured feature importance by comparing them with a retrain-based ablation benchmark, in which each feature was removed in turn and the NPE retrained. We considered two jointly trained gates: independent sigmoid weights and competing softmax weights. If these reliably reflect feature importance, they should align with the ablation-based estimates. Across nine independent training seeds, however, gate-based and ablation-based importance were negatively correlated (Spearman's rho approximately -0.61 for sigmoid gating and -0.56 for softmax gating). The feature that ablation identified as most important, total signal power, was among the features the gate down-weighted most, despite gating costing negligible predictive accuracy. These results extend a pattern previously documented for attention mechanisms in natural language processing and for explainability methods in electroencephalography (EEG) deep learning to the simulation-based inference setting, and suggest caution when interpreting learned gate weights as measures of causal feature importance in scientific machine-learning pipelines.

AI.tldr: Learned gate weights in an NPE-based simulation-based inference pipeline do not reflect causal feature importance; they are negatively correlated with retrain-based ablation importance.
AI.motivation: SBI fits mechanistic models to data but offers little insight into which data features drive inferred parameters, so cheap interpretability methods such as learned feature gates are attractive—yet this assumes predictive training reveals input importance.
AI.method: In a computational neuroscience setting, neural posterior estimation infers four physiological parameters of the Jansen-Rit model. Two jointly trained gates (independent sigmoid weights, competing softmax weights) were compared against a retrain-based ablation benchmark, where each feature was removed and NPE retrained, across nine seeds.
AI.result: Gate-based and ablation-based importance were negatively correlated (Spearman rho about -0.61 for sigmoid, -0.56 for softmax). Total signal power, the most important feature by ablation, was among the most down-weighted by gates, despite negligible accuracy cost.
AI.conclusion: The findings extend prior warnings from attention in NLP and EEG deep-learning explainability to SBI, and caution against interpreting learned gate weights as causal feature importance in scientific machine-learning pipelines.

title: Modelling Toxin-Induced Intraspecific Personality Variation in Predator-Prey Dynamics
comment: 38 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to Journal of Theoretical Biology
summary: Personality traits, such as boldness and shyness, can affect interspecific interactions through differences in individual behaviour. Environmental toxins may also alter these traits. However, few predator-prey models have considered animal personality. In this study, we extend a toxin-dependent predator-prey model by incorporating personality variation in both prey and predators. Prey personality affects birth and growth, whereas predator personality affects the predator functional response. The model is parameterized for rainbow trout and aquatic insect prey exposed to methylmercury. Numerical results show that prey and predator personality have different effects on population dynamics. Prey personality tends to reduce biomass fluctuations and promote stable coexistence. In contrast, predator personality can increase biomass fluctuations and lead to persistent population oscillations. These effects are mainly observed at low and intermediate toxin concentrations that are environmentally relevant to freshwater ecosystems. Using a quasi-steady-state approximation, we reduce the model to a two-dimensional system and study its positivity, boundedness, and the existence of equilibria. The equilibrium structure depends jointly on the toxin level and the prey and predator personality contrasts. Based on this existence classification, we numerically investigate the local stability of all feasible equilibria and identify parameter regions corresponding to locally stable extinction, prey-only persistence, coexistence, and bistability. Overall, toxin-induced personality variation can qualitatively change predator-prey dynamics.

AI.tldr: The authors extend a toxin-dependent predator-prey model by adding personality variation (boldness/shyness) in both prey and predator, parameterized for rainbow trout and aquatic insect prey exposed to methylmercury, and analyze how toxin-induced personality variation qualitatively changes population dynamics.
AI.motivation: Personality traits such as boldness and shyness affect interspecific interactions, and environmental toxins may alter these traits, yet few predator-prey models account for animal personality. The paper aims to fill this gap by linking toxin exposure, personality variation, and population dynamics.
AI.method: A toxin-dependent predator-prey model is extended with personality variation: prey personality affects birth and growth, predator personality affects the functional response. The model is parameterized for rainbow trout and aquatic insect prey under methylmercury exposure. A quasi-steady-state approximation reduces it to a two-dimensional system, whose positivity, boundedness, and equilibria are analyzed; then local stability of all feasible equilibria is examined numerically to map parameter regions.
AI.result: Prey and predator personality have different effects: prey personality reduces biomass fluctuations and promotes stable coexistence, whereas predator personality increases fluctuations and leads to persistent oscillations. These effects occur mainly at low and intermediate, environmentally relevant toxin concentrations. The equilibrium structure depends jointly on toxin level and prey/predator personality contrasts, yielding regions of locally stable extinction, prey-only persistence, coexistence, and bistability.
AI.conclusion: Toxin-induced personality variation can qualitatively change predator-prey dynamics, highlighting the importance of incorporating behavioral/personality heterogeneity into ecotoxicological population models.

title: Shorter but not more catalytic: an active-site-resolved model of how tau reshapes amyloid-$β$ secondary nucleation
summary: Tau cross-seeding creates a mechanistic puzzle. Tau fibrils accelerate amyloid-$β$42 (A$β$42) nucleation and produce a larger population of shorter A$β$ fibrils, yet homotypic secondary nucleation occurs at rare catalytic sites rather than uniformly over fibril mass. Does making more, shorter fibrils make the A$β$ population more catalytic? A coupled tau-A$β$ model is extended to track fibril number, fibril mass, total active secondary-nucleation sites, and the fraction of sites exposed after plaque consolidation. The model recovers the preceding plaque-surface-limited formulation when active sites form in direct proportion to fibril mass. At matched fibril mass, shortening alone has little effect: the departure of active-site density from mass proportionality scales inversely with mean fibril size, so the extra fibrils matter only if each birth event introduces about as many sites as elongation adds over a mean-length fibril. At equal time, the sign of the homotypic response is controlled mainly by a Damkohler number comparing monomer consumption by elongation with monomer clearance. Tau coupling increases homotypic secondary nucleation while clearance controls free monomer, but suppresses it once elongation becomes the dominant monomer sink. In a composite scenario, these regimes occur in sequence. Across all cases examined, including 800 Latin-hypercube samples and simulations with mean fibril lengths of 0.3-30 $μm$, direct tau catalysis increases accumulated oligomer-equivalent exposure. The model predicts that shorter tau-seeded fibrils are not intrinsically more catalytic unless their sites are more numerous per unit mass, more active, or more exposed; matched-mass site counting and secondary-nucleation measurements can distinguish these alternatives.

AI.tldr: A coupled tau–Aβ model tracking fibril number, mass, active secondary-nucleation sites, and exposed-site fraction shows that tau-seeded fibrils being shorter does not intrinsically make the Aβ population more catalytic; the homotypic response instead depends on site density per mass and on a Damköhler number comparing elongation-driven monomer consumption to clearance.
AI.motivation: Tau fibrils accelerate Aβ42 nucleation and yield more, shorter Aβ fibrils, yet homotypic secondary nucleation occurs at rare catalytic sites rather than uniformly over fibril mass. The open question is whether producing more, shorter fibrils actually makes the Aβ population more catalytic.
AI.method: Extends a coupled tau–Aβ kinetic model to track fibril number, fibril mass, total active secondary-nucleation sites, and the fraction of sites exposed after plaque consolidation. The model reduces to a prior plaque-surface-limited formulation when active sites scale with fibril mass. Analysis includes a Damköhler number (elongation monomer consumption vs. monomer clearance), 800 Latin-hypercube samples, and mean fibril lengths of 0.3–30 μm.
AI.result: At matched fibril mass, shortening alone has little effect: departure of active-site density from mass proportionality scales inversely with mean fibril size, so extra fibrils matter only if each birth event adds roughly as many sites as elongation adds over a mean-length fibril. At equal time, the sign of the homotypic response is set mainly by the Damköhler number; tau coupling raises homotypic secondary nucleation while clearance controls free monomer, but suppresses it once elongation dominates monomer consumption. These regimes occur sequentially in a composite scenario. Across all cases, direct tau catalysis increases accumulated oligomer-equivalent exposure.
AI.conclusion: Shorter tau-seeded fibrils are not intrinsically more catalytic unless their sites are more numerous per unit mass, more active, or more exposed. Matched-mass site counting combined with secondary-nucleation measurements can distinguish these alternatives.

title: Report the tolerance, not the count: exact phylogenetic distance deconvolution with incomplete references
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures. Supplementary appendices (32 pages) are included as an ancillary file. Code, exact input fixtures and saved run records: https://github.com/Haotian-Tang/recomb2027-pdd
summary:
Phylogenetic distance deconvolution represents mixture-to-reference distances by weighted sources placed on a reference tree. We study the minimum number of strictly interior sources that explains a distance profile, and what incomplete references cost.
  On a positive-rational reduced tree we give an exact algorithm with 2^O(K) poly(B) bit complexity for a free positive mean pendant and any nonempty set of observed leaves. With arbitrary missing references and a prescribed pendant the problem is W[1]-hard in the source budget K, even on positive binary trees supplied with a strict explanation using at most K+1 sources.
  We then use the algorithm as an instrument. Removing references can only lower the minimum source count, never raise it. The direction is a theorem at every error tolerance and held without exception in 23,545 draws, so which references are missing matters more than how many. Two adversarially chosen references suffice, at the median, to destroy uniqueness of the minimum explanation, and that number does not grow with panel size (Spearman 0.203, p = 0.15, over 20 to 353 references) where random loss scales linearly. Discarding 7,931 of 10,575 references from a real 16S panel at random costs 1.8% of the tolerance at which one source suffices. Discarding comparably many as whole clades costs 90%.
  That tolerance needs neither ground truth nor an error model, which makes the model measurable on real data. Published distance estimates exceed it in 296 of 296 cases. The mixture inferred by the published heuristic reproduces real observations better than the configuration that generated them in 282 of 296. The phenomenon is not unobservable in practice. It is unobservable through a point estimate of the count. Methods for this problem should report the tolerance at which an explanation of a given size exists.

AI.tldr: The paper studies phylogenetic distance deconvolution—representing mixture-to-reference distances via weighted sources on a reference tree—and analyzes the minimum number of strictly interior sources needed to explain a distance profile, along with the cost of incomplete references.
AI.motivation: To understand the minimum number of interior sources explaining a distance profile and how missing references affect this, since which references are missing matters more than how many.
AI.method: An exact algorithm with 2^O(K) poly(B) bit complexity on positive-rational reduced trees (free positive mean pendant, any observed leaves); W[1]-hardness in source budget K for arbitrary missing references with prescribed pendant. Empirical instrument: removing references, adversarial vs random loss, tolerance-based measures on synthetic draws and a real 16S panel.
AI.result: Removing references can only lower the minimum source count (a theorem held in all 23,545 draws). Two adversarial references suffice to destroy uniqueness at the median, independent of panel size (Spearman 0.203, p=0.15), while random loss scales linearly. Discarding 7,931/10,575 references randomly costs 1.8% of tolerance; whole clades cost 90%. Published distance estimates exceed the tolerance in 296/296 cases; the published heuristic mixture reproduces observations better than the generating configuration in 282/296.
AI.conclusion: The phenomenon is unobservable through a point estimate of the source count. Methods should report the tolerance at which an explanation of a given size exists, which needs neither ground truth nor an error model and is measurable on real data.

title: From Turing Patterns to Spike Self-Replication and Nucleation in a Growing-Domain Tulip Breaking Virus Model
summary: A recently proposed reaction-diffusion model for the tulip breaking virus (TBV) has been shown to generate striped pigmentation patterns on growing tulip petals. In this paper, we investigate the formation of localized spike patterns in this model in the asymptotic limit of small viral diffusivity. It is known that two distinct bifurcation mechanisms can occur which generate new spikes as the domain half-length $L$ slowly increases: spike self-replication and spike nucleation. Self-replication occurs through a saddle-node bifurcation of the inner spike core problem, whereas nucleation is associated with a fold of the nonlinear outer problem. Using matched asymptotic expansions, we derive critical conditions for these mechanisms and construct phase diagrams that predict which mechanism occurs first as $L$ increases, or whether nucleation is absent. We further combine these results with a Turing instability analysis of the homogeneous steady state to obtain a phase diagram of pattern-forming mechanisms. An interesting finding is that, for the TBV model, the Turing-unstable region lies entirely within the parameter regime where spike nucleation is possible. These results provide further insight into the mechanisms underlying the formation and evolution of pigmentation patterns in virus-infected tulips.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes localized spike pattern formation in a reaction-diffusion model for tulip breaking virus (TBV) pigmentation, in the asymptotic limit of small viral diffusivity. Using matched asymptotic expansions, it derives critical conditions distinguishing spike self-replication (saddle-node bifurcation of the inner core problem) from nucleation (fold of the nonlinear outer problem) as the domain half-length L increases.
AI.motivation: A recent reaction-diffusion model generates striped pigmentation on growing tulip petals via TBV, but how localized spike patterns form and evolve as the domain grows, and which bifurcation mechanism dominates, remained unclear. Understanding these mechanisms could explain pattern formation and evolution in virus-infected tulips.
AI.method: Matched asymptotic expansions in the limit of small viral diffusivity, deriving critical conditions for spike self-replication and spike nucleation. Constructs phase diagrams predicting which mechanism occurs first as L increases (or whether nucleation is absent), and combines these with a Turing instability analysis of the homogeneous steady state to obtain a phase diagram of pattern-forming mechanisms.
AI.result: Critical conditions and phase diagrams distinguish self-replication from nucleation and identify when nucleation is absent. Notably, for the TBV model, the Turing-unstable region lies entirely within the parameter regime where spike nucleation is possible.
AI.conclusion: The analysis clarifies the bifurcation mechanisms governing localized spike patterns in the TBV model and their interplay with Turing instability, providing insight into the formation and evolution of tulip pigmentation patterns.

title: Music Between Two Minds: Individual Signatures, Shared States, and the Emergence of Creative Interaction
summary: Some of the most valued forms of human creativity arise between people-in conversation, collaboration, and improvised music-yet how two minds jointly regulate the flow of novelty in real time remains unknown. Here we examined the information dynamics of interpersonal improvisation using 986 professional jazz improvisations. Pitch-based fluctuations of uncertainty and surprise behaved as signatures of individual identity: the two partners differed within 90% of takes, performers were identifiable from single solos and the separation between partners persisted undiminished across turns and takes. Rhythm-based fluctuations showed the reverse organization: partners were statistically indistinguishable within a take yet shifted together from take to take, and this shared state drifted gradually as each performance progressed, with each performer moving away from their own past at the same rate as from their partner's. Beyond joint drift, solo hand-offs revealed turn-by-turn complementarity: when one performer exceeded their own average surprise in the predictive dynamics of improvisation, the partner's next solo fell below their own, in both pitch and rhythm and in all duos. Improvising pairs thus neither fuse into one system nor remain two independent ones: they preserve individual melodic voices while sharing a rhythmic state, within which moment-to-moment push-pull continually rebalances their interaction. Individuality and togetherness thus coexist, carried by different musical dimensions, a measurable organization of creativity that emerges between minds.

AI.tldr: In 986 professional jazz duo improvisations, pitch-based surprise/uncertainty signatures identified which performer was playing (distinct individual voices), while rhythm-based fluctuations were shared and drifted together between partners; in addition, a performer's above-average surprise was followed by below-average surprise in the partner's next solo, revealing turn-by-turn complementarity.
AI.motivation: Highly valued human creativity—conversation, collaboration, improvised music—arises between people, yet how two minds jointly regulate the flow of novelty in real time is unknown. The paper asks whether joint improvisation fuses partners into one system or keeps them as two independent ones.
AI.method: Analysis of information dynamics (fluctuations of uncertainty and surprise) in 986 professional jazz improvisations, computed separately for pitch and rhythm; performer identifiability, within- versus across-take separation, joint drift over a performance, and turn-by-turn (solo hand-off) dependencies were examined.
AI.result: Pitch dynamics behaved as an individual signature: partners differed within 90% of takes, performers were identifiable from single solos, and the separation persisted undiminished across turns and takes. Rhythm dynamics showed the reverse: partners were statistically indistinguishable within a take but shifted together between takes, drifting gradually as performance progressed, each performer moving from their own past at the same rate as from their partner's. Solo hand-offs showed complementarity in both pitch and rhythm and in all duos: when one performer exceeded their own average surprise, the partner's next solo fell below theirs.
AI.conclusion: Improvising pairs neither fuse into a single system nor remain two independent ones: they preserve individual melodic voices while sharing a rhythmic state, within which moment-to-moment push-pull continuously rebalances interaction. Individuality and togetherness coexist, carried by different musical dimensions—a measurable organization of creativity that emerges between minds.

title: Generalized modeling reveals stabilizing mechanisms in cross-feeding microbial communities
summary: Understanding what makes microbial communities stable and able to resist perturbation is a fundamental question in microbial ecology. Theoretical approaches to this problem typically require making strict assumptions about the structure, parameters and functional forms used in models, hindering general insight. Here, we address this problem by developing and analyzing a generalized model of microbial community dynamics, capturing resource-mediated competitive and cross-feeding interactions between populations. The generalized modeling approach allows us to assess the stability of microbial systems across large ensembles of models with variable size, structure and non-linear dynamics. Our analysis shows how community stability is constrained by system size and identifies its key metabolic and dynamical drivers, highlighting the central roles of self-limitation, metabolic efficiency and plasticity. Furthermore, we show how the structure of communities mediates their stability, allowing communities to counteract the destabilizing cross-feeding loops through organization into hierarchical trophic structures. Together, these results provide new insight into the stability of microbial communities and offer a flexible analytical framework for future work to explore the responses of communities to perturbation.

AI.tldr: Using a generalized model of resource-mediated microbial community dynamics, the authors show that stability is constrained by system size and driven by self-limitation, metabolic efficiency, and plasticity, with hierarchical trophic organization counteracting destabilizing cross-feeding loops.
AI.motivation: Understanding what makes microbial communities stable and resistant to perturbation is a fundamental question in microbial ecology. Existing theoretical approaches typically impose strict assumptions on model structure, parameters, and functional forms, which prevents general insight.
AI.method: Develops and analyzes a generalized model of microbial community dynamics capturing resource-mediated competitive and cross-feeding interactions between populations. The generalized modeling approach assesses stability across large ensembles of models with variable size, structure, and nonlinear dynamics.
AI.result: Community stability is constrained by system size; key metabolic and dynamical drivers are identified, highlighting central roles of self-limitation, metabolic efficiency, and plasticity. Community structure mediates stability, allowing communities to counteract destabilizing cross-feeding loops via hierarchical trophic organization.
AI.conclusion: The results provide new insight into microbial community stability and offer a flexible analytical framework for exploring community responses to perturbation.

title: Benchmarking Recent Single-Cell Synthetic Data Generation Methods on the OneK1K Dataset
comment: 6 pages, presented at CAMDA 2026 ELSA Health Privacy Challenge
summary: Synthetic single-cell RNA-seq data generation offers a promising route for privacy-aware biomedical data sharing, but donor-linked datasets require careful balancing of biological utility and privacy risk. In this work, we benchmark synthetic generation methods for the CAMDA 2026 ELSA Health Privacy Challenge using the donor-split OneK1K dataset, comparing scGFT, scLDM, and Cell2Sentence across statistical fidelity, downstream biological preservation, and membership inference vulnerability. Because full-transcriptome generation is computationally demanding, we focus generative modeling on highly variable genes and evaluate alternative strategies for reconstructing non-HVG expression. Our results show that non-HVG handling is a central determinant of privacy: directly copying non-HVG values leads to severe leakage, whereas Poisson-based reconstruction substantially reduces membership inference risk. We further find that scGFT and scLDM better preserve biological structure than an independent Poisson baseline, while maintaining near-random privacy profiles under appropriate configurations. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating synthetic single-cell data beyond marginal similarity alone, emphasizing robustness, interpretability, and privacy-conscious design choices throughout preprocessing, generation, and post-processing.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks synthetic scRNA-seq generation methods (scGFT, scLDM, Cell2Sentence) on donor-split OneK1K for the CAMDA 2026 ELSA Health Privacy Challenge, showing that how non-HVG genes are reconstructed dominates membership-inference privacy risk, and that Poisson-based reconstruction plus generative modeling of HVGs preserves biology while limiting leakage.
AI.motivation: Synthetic single-cell RNA-seq offers privacy-aware data sharing, but donor-linked datasets demand a balance between biological utility and privacy risk. The authors need to assess where that trade-off actually breaks down across generation pipelines.
AI.method: Uses the donor-split OneK1K dataset. Compares scGFT, scLDM, and Cell2Sentence on statistical fidelity, downstream biological preservation, and membership inference vulnerability. To manage computational cost, generative modeling is restricted to highly variable genes, with separate strategies evaluated for reconstructing non-HVG expression (direct copying vs. Poisson-based reconstruction), against an independent Poisson baseline.
AI.result: Non-HVG handling is the central determinant of privacy: directly copying non-HVG values causes severe leakage, whereas Poisson-based reconstruction substantially reduces membership inference risk. scGFT and scLDM better preserve biological structure than the independent Poisson baseline while maintaining near-random privacy profiles under suitable configurations. Marginal similarity alone does not capture these differences.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic single-cell data must be evaluated beyond marginal distributional similarity, with attention to robustness, interpretability, and privacy-conscious choices across preprocessing, generation, and post-processing—especially in how non-HVG expression is handled.

title: Dynamics of random recurrent neural networks: colored noise and sublinear activations
summary: We study the dynamics of recurrent neural networks with random couplings, sublinear odd activation functions, and temporally correlated noise. Using large N methods, we determine stationary correlations and distinguish the loss of local linear stability from the onset of chaos, characterized by a positive largest Lyapunov exponent. These thresholds delimit an intermediate regime in which local instability coexists with asymptotic stability under a common noise history. Their separation depends on both the noise correlation time and the asymptotic growth of the activation function. We show that internal noise with any finite correlation time cuts off the divergence of the network's intrinsic correlation time tau_corr at the edge of chaos; it exhibits a critical scaling tau_{corr,max} propto 1/sqrt{D_0}, where D_0 is the integrated noise strength. Static random input instead produces coincident thresholds and a divergent correlation time. We also calculate the frequency-dependent participation dimension from a four-point correlation function. Its zero-frequency value is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the network correlation time, predicting a smooth minimum at the weak-noise chaos threshold. Numerical simulations support the large-network predictions and reveal appreciable finite-size effects.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes random recurrent neural networks with sublinear odd activations and temporally correlated noise, using large-N methods to distinguish local linear instability from the onset of chaos and to characterize an intermediate regime and noise-dependent critical scaling.
AI.motivation: Prior work conflates loss of local linear stability with the onset of chaotic dynamics (positive largest Lyapunov exponent). The authors aim to separate these transitions and understand how temporally correlated internal noise versus static random input shapes the network's dynamics, correlation time, and participation dimension near the edge of chaos.
AI.method: Large-N (mean-field) analysis of recurrent networks with random couplings, sublinear odd activation functions, and temporally correlated noise. The authors compute stationary correlations, largest Lyapunov exponents, intrinsic correlation time tau_corr, and frequency-dependent participation dimension from a four-point correlation function, supported by numerical simulations probing finite-size effects.
AI.result: Local instability and chaos onset are distinct thresholds delimiting an intermediate regime where local instability coexists with asymptotic stability under a common noise history. The separation depends on noise correlation time and activation growth. Any finite-correlation-time internal noise cuts off the divergence of tau_corr at the edge of chaos, with tau_{corr,max} ∝ 1/sqrt{D_0} (D_0 = integrated noise strength), whereas static random input yields coincident thresholds and divergent tau_corr. The zero-frequency participation dimension scales inversely with the fourth power of network correlation time, predicting a smooth minimum at the weak-noise chaos threshold.
AI.conclusion: Internal noise with finite correlation time fundamentally changes the edge-of-chaos phenomenology by separating instability from chaos and regularizing the correlation-time divergence, in contrast to static input. Large-network predictions are confirmed numerically, with appreciable finite-size effects.

title: ProMORNA: An End-to-End Generative Framework for Full-Length mRNA Design
summary: Designing therapeutic messenger RNA (mRNA) requires generating full-length transcripts that optimally balance intracellular stability and translation efficiency. While generative models have advanced mRNA design, existing approaches rely on region-wise generation, expensive inference-time search, or target-specific model updates. To overcome these limitations, we introduce ProMORNA, a zero-shot, end-to-end generative framework for full-length mRNA design. ProMORNA aligns the design process with modern Large Language Model training pipelines: it utilizes a BART-style architecture pre-trained on over 6 million natural protein-mRNA pairs, followed by a two-stage post-training process comprising cold-start supervised fine-tuning and multi-objective reinforcement learning. By standardizing and aggregating relative advantages at the individual metric level with domain-specific stabilization, our post-training stage directly aligns the generative policy with conflicting biological constraints while avoiding direct scalarization of raw objective scores. In silico evaluations demonstrate that ProMORNA pushes the Pareto frontier of predicted stability and translation efficiency beyond standard baselines and GEMORNA, a leading state-of-the-art method. In three independent in vitro Fluc2P experiments, Candidate 2 achieved a 12-72h reporter-activity AUC 3.33 times that of the conventional Benchmark (Holm-adjusted $P=0.01285$), while its estimated 1.29-fold advantage over the reported best GEMORNA candidate remained exploratory. These results support ProMORNA as a promising framework for generating functionally active full-length mRNA candidates.

AI.tldr: ProMORNA is a zero-shot end-to-end generative framework for full-length mRNA design that adapts LLM-style training (BART pre-training on 6M protein-mRNA pairs, cold-start SFT, multi-objective RL) to jointly optimize stability and translation efficiency.
AI.motivation: Therapeutic mRNA design needs full-length transcripts that balance intracellular stability and translation efficiency. Existing generative approaches are limited by region-wise generation, costly inference-time search, or target-specific model updates, so a general, efficient full-length generator is needed.
AI.method: ProMORNA uses a BART-style architecture pre-trained on over 6 million natural protein-mRNA pairs, followed by two-stage post-training: cold-start supervised fine-tuning and multi-objective reinforcement learning. It standardizes and aggregates relative advantages at the individual-metric level with domain-specific stabilization, aligning the policy to conflicting biological constraints without scalarizing raw objective scores.
AI.result: In silico, ProMORNA pushes the Pareto frontier of predicted stability and translation efficiency beyond baselines and GEMORNA. In three independent in vitro Fluc2P experiments, Candidate 2 achieved a 12-72h reporter-activity AUC 3.33x that of the conventional Benchmark (Holm-adjusted P=0.01285); a 1.29-fold advantage over the best reported GEMORNA candidate remained exploratory.
AI.conclusion: ProMORNA is a promising zero-shot end-to-end framework for generating functionally active full-length mRNA candidates, with strong in silico and initial in vitro support, though comparison against the best GEMORNA candidate requires further validation.

title: QProtFuse: Query-Guided Layer Fusion for Retrieval-Augmented Protein Function Prediction
summary: Predicting protein functions from amino acid sequences is essential to understanding biological processes. Large language models (LLMs) offer flexible function descriptions to natural-language queries, yet their limited protein understanding motivates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Existing protein RAG methods primarily expand external retrieval signals while overlooking the rich knowledge encoded within a single protein language model (PLM). We show that retrieval performance varies across PLM layers and biological tasks, making conventional final-layer selection suboptimal. To this end, we propose QProtFuse, which uses queries to adaptively fuse multi-layer protein features and jointly learns protein and annotation retrieval through intra-modal and cross-modal contrastive objectives. On Prot-Inst-OOD, QProtFuse achieves the best protein and annotation retrieval scores, reaching 16.4\% Recall@1 with annotation reranking. These gains improve downstream RAG-based function descriptions, yielding the highest LLM-as-a-judge scores for both Qwen3-8B (6.22/10) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (6.68/10). Ablations and weight analyses demonstrate the value of query-guided fusion and complementary training objectives for exploiting a PLM's internal knowledge.

AI.tldr: QProtFuse is a protein RAG retriever that uses queries to adaptively fuse multi-layer protein language model features and jointly learns protein and annotation retrieval via intra- and cross-modal contrastive objectives, improving retrieval and downstream LLM function descriptions.
AI.motivation: Predicting protein function from sequences matters for biology, and RAG can augment LLMs that lack protein understanding. Existing protein RAG methods focus on adding external retrieval signals while ignoring the rich knowledge already inside a single PLM. Moreover, retrieval performance varies by PLM layer and task, so using only the final layer is suboptimal.
AI.method: QProtFuse adaptively fuses multi-layer protein features conditioned on the query, and jointly trains protein and annotation retrieval using intra-modal and cross-modal contrastive objectives.
AI.result: On Prot-Inst-OOD, QProtFuse achieves the best protein and annotation retrieval scores, reaching 16.4% Recall@1 with annotation reranking. Downstream RAG-based function descriptions also improve, giving the highest LLM-as-a-judge scores for Qwen3-8B (6.22/10) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (6.68/10). Ablations and weight analyses confirm the value of query-guided fusion and complementary training objectives.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting a PLM's internal multi-layer knowledge through query-guided fusion, combined with joint protein/annotation contrastive training, enhances protein retrieval and the quality of RAG-generated function descriptions.

title: AI Mindmeld: A Latent Interconnect Protocol
summary:
LLMs can act as scientific agents using tools to consult specialists and run experiments. Yet specialist information must enter their context, generally as text, images, audio or video: a bottleneck between models with rich, high-dimensional representations. We advocate direct representation exchange: a mindmeld conveying many properties, including information an LLM would not think to request. It should be extensible to new specialists, flexible across questions and tasks, and compositional across independently connected specialists without joint training.
  The Latent Interconnect Protocol (LIP) learns connectors mapping specialist representations into LLM internal states. Training only connectors keeps this practical as LLMs grow and evolve. We connect three protein and three small molecule specialists to Gemma 3 (4B and 12B parameters) and Kimi K2.6 (1T total, 32B active), freezing all pretrained models. Independently trained connectors provide useful information without changing the LLM or existing connectors, supporting familiar and new question types about unseen objects. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer to cross-domain tasks without joint training. Task performance and compositionality generally improve with LLM capability, with especially strong gains in zero-shot task transfer. Limitations remain: current LLMs were not trained for specialist representations as native inputs; access does not ensure reliable interpretation, integration or use in reasoning. We call on specialist developers to provide consistent representation interfaces and, especially, on LLM developers to train models to receive, combine and reason with these inputs. These efforts could expand scientific agents' information while preserving conventional tools' flexibility.
  Data, pretrained connectors, and code for training, evaluation and interactive inference: https://github.com/PolymathicAI/AI-Mindmeld

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "mindmeld" — direct exchange of specialist representations — and the Latent Interconnect Protocol (LIP), which trains lightweight connectors mapping specialist model representations into LLM internal states while freezing pretrained models, enabling zero-shot cross-domain transfer and composability.
AI.motivation: LLM scientific agents currently receive specialist information only through text/images/audio/video, creating a bottleneck that loses rich, high-dimensional specialist representations and excludes information the LLM wouldn't think to request.
AI.method: LIP trains only connectors that map specialist representations into LLM internal states, keeping all pretrained models frozen. Three protein and three small-molecule specialists are connected to Gemma 3 (4B, 12B) and Kimi K2.6 (1T total, 32B active); connectors are trained independently, and the design is extensible, flexible across questions/tasks, and compositional.
AI.result: Independently trained connectors supply useful information without altering the LLM or existing connectors, supporting familiar and new question types about unseen objects. Zero-shot transfer to cross-domain tasks works without joint training. Task performance and compositionality improve with LLM capability, especially in zero-shot transfer. Limitations: current LLMs weren't trained on specialist representations as native inputs, and access does not guarantee reliable interpretation, integration, or reasoning use.
AI.conclusion: The authors call on specialist developers to provide consistent representation interfaces and on LLM developers to train models to receive, combine, and reason with such inputs, expanding scientific agents' information while preserving tool flexibility. Code, data, and pretrained connectors are released.

title: Non-Destructive Detection of Early Drought Stress via Spectral Submanifold Analysis
comment: Includes supplementary information and one supplementary video. This manuscript has been submitted
summary: Non-destructive early detection of water stress is critical for precision agriculture, yet current detection methods are often labor-intensive or destructive. We propose a rapid, non-invasive method based on Spectral Submanifold (SSM) reduction to analyze the nonlinear vibration dynamics of soybean plants. Unlike traditional linear modal analysis, our data-driven approach reveals a distinct transition in the dominant dynamics of the plant stem as drought progresses. Specifically, we uncover a sign reversal in the nonlinear damping coefficient within SSM-reduced models of full plants. Our finding reveals a fundamental transition in the plant's dissipative mechanics from a pressurized, fluid-rich vessel exhibiting superlinear (viscoelastic) damping to a dry, cellular solid dominated by sublinear (frictional) damping. This transition is closely correlated with the onset of physiological stress indicated by a significant decrease in the values of mature-leaf soil plant analysis development (SPAD) and colorimetric metrics. In contrast, traditional metrics, such as linear frequency and leaf wilting, do not provide consistent statistical signals of water stress. This study provides the first experimental evidence that SSM-based nonlinear model reduction can detect the changing internal state of a living organism, offering a physics-based metric for high-throughput plant phenotyping.

AI.tldr: A data-driven Spectral Submanifold (SSM) reduction of soybean stem vibrations reveals a sign reversal in the nonlinear damping coefficient as drought progresses, offering a non-destructive physics-based metric for early water-stress detection.
AI.motivation: Early detection of water stress in crops is important for precision agriculture, but existing methods are labor-intensive or destructive. Traditional linear vibration metrics (frequency, wilting) also fail to give consistent statistical signals of drought stress.
AI.method: The authors apply SSM-based nonlinear model reduction to the vibration dynamics of full soybean plants, fitting SSM-reduced models to extract nonlinear damping coefficients, and compare these against physiological indicators (SPAD values and colorimetric metrics).
AI.result: The dominant stem dynamics show a clear transition during drought, marked by a sign reversal of the nonlinear damping coefficient: plants shift from superlinear (viscoelastic) damping in pressurized, fluid-rich tissue to sublinear (frictional) damping in dry cellular solid. This transition correlates with decreased SPAD and colorimetric stress metrics, whereas linear frequency and leaf wilting do not yield consistent statistical signals.
AI.conclusion: This is the first experimental evidence that SSM-based nonlinear model reduction can detect changing internal states of a living organism, providing a physics-based, non-destructive metric suitable for high-throughput plant phenotyping.

title: Escaping the Phylogenetic Trap: Persistent Homology Enables Cross-Species Ion Channel Classification via Multimodal Graph Neural Networks
summary: Protein classifiers are highly sensitive to evaluation protocol: random train/test splits induce phylogenetic leakage, allowing models to exploit taxon-specific correlations and substantially overestimate out-of-distribution performance. This issue is particularly acute for venom compound classification by ion-channel target (Ca2+, K+, Na+), where reported accuracies of 80-90% do not reflect generalization to unseen taxa. We formulate cross-species prediction as a structured distribution shift in which taxonomic identity acts as a confounder, requiring representations that capture structural features invariant across phylogeny. Using a shared multimodal backbone that fuses ESM-2 sequence embeddings with a disulfide-aware graph attention network, we systematically compare five structural inductive biases (spectral, Riemannian, SE(3)-invariant, statistical-manifold, and persistent-homology representations) under a leave-one-taxon-out evaluation protocol on a benchmark of 1,373 ColabFold-predicted venom compounds spanning five taxa. The persistent-homology representation summarizes backbone geometry through topological descriptors that are robust to local structural perturbations, providing an inductive bias toward phylogenetically invariant learning. Under conventional i.i.d. splits, all models achieve similar accuracy (81-86%), masking differences in inductive bias. Under taxonomic shift, this parity collapses: a sequence-only baseline drops to approximately 30%, the remaining geometric priors cluster at 54-55%, while our persistent-homology model (PH-GNN) achieves 63.4%, outperforming the next-best method by over 8 percentage points. These results demonstrate that random-split evaluation obscures meaningful differences in representation quality and identify topological representations as an effective inductive bias for learning under structured biological distribution shift.

AI.tldr: Random train/test splits in protein classifier evaluation cause phylogenetic leakage that inflates accuracy; under leave-one-taxon-out evaluation, a persistent-homology graph neural network (PH-GNN) reaches 63.4% versus ~30% for sequence-only and 54-55% for other geometric priors, showing topology is a strong inductive bias for taxonomic shift.
AI.motivation: Reported 80-90% accuracies for venom compound ion-channel target classification (Ca2+, K+, Na+) are inflated by random splits that leak phylogenetic information, so models exploit taxon-specific correlations and fail to generalize to unseen taxa. Cross-species prediction should be framed as a structured distribution shift where taxonomic identity is a confounder, demanding phylogenetically invariant representations.
AI.method: A shared multimodal backbone fusing ESM-2 sequence embeddings with a disulfide-aware graph attention network is used to compare five structural inductive biases (spectral, Riemannian, SE(3)-invariant, statistical-manifold, persistent-homology) under a leave-one-taxon-out protocol on a benchmark of 1,373 ColabFold-predicted venom compounds across five taxa. The persistent-homology model summarizes backbone geometry via topological descriptors robust to local perturbations.
AI.result: Under i.i.d. splits all models score similarly (81-86%), masking inductive-bias differences. Under taxonomic shift the sequence-only baseline drops to ~30%, other geometric priors cluster at 54-55%, and PH-GNN achieves 63.4%, exceeding the next-best by over 8 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Random-split evaluation obscures meaningful differences in representation quality; topological (persistent-homology) representations are an effective inductive bias for learning under structured biological distribution shift and should inform future cross-species protein classification benchmarks.

title: Supercoiling Drives DNA-Protein Co-Condensation
summary: The co-condensation of DNA and proteins plays an important role in genome compaction, including heterochromatin formation and chromosome segregation. Meanwhile, transcription and replication continuously generate DNA supercoiling, yet how the resulting torsional stress affects co-condensation remains poorly understood. Here, by coupling DNA elasticity to a protein concentration field, we show that supercoiling acts as a topological catalyst for co-condensation through a mutually reinforcing interplay with protein wetting. Specifically, protein wetting facilitates twist-to-writhe conversion, generating highly writhed DNA conformations that in turn promote capillary collapse into a protein-rich droplet. In the absence of supercoiling, DNA remains kinetically trapped in metastable extended states within our model, whereas sufficiently strong supercoiling removes the nucleation barrier and enables spontaneous co-condensation. These results establish topology as a distinct control parameter for biomolecular condensation and provide a mechanical framework for how active genomic processes can dynamically regulate large-scale genome organization.

AI.tldr: Supercoiling acts as a topological catalyst for DNA-protein co-condensation via a positive feedback loop with protein wetting.
AI.motivation: DNA-protein co-condensation is key to genome compaction, and transcription/replication generate DNA supercoiling, but how torsional stress affects co-condensation is poorly understood.
AI.method: A theoretical model coupling DNA elasticity to a protein concentration field, capturing twist-to-writhe conversion and protein wetting.
AI.result: Protein wetting promotes twist-to-writhe conversion producing highly writhed DNA that drives capillary collapse into droplets; without supercoiling DNA stays kinetically trapped in metastable extended states, while strong supercoiling removes the nucleation barrier enabling spontaneous co-condensation.
AI.conclusion: Topology is a distinct control parameter for biomolecular condensation, offering a mechanical framework for how active genomic processes dynamically regulate large-scale genome organization.

title: RiboBridge: protein-conditioned de novo RNA binder structure design
summary: Designing RNA molecules that bind to target protein structures requires generating both an RNA conformation and its bound complex geometry, without assuming a predefined binding site. Existing approaches generally model these coupled processes within a unified representation, entangling RNA conformation generation with protein-relative placement. In this work, we introduce RiboBridge, a structure-first framework that separates RNA conformational generation from protein--RNA assembly through cross-frame interaction geometry. RiboBridge first proposes multiple candidate RNA-binding interfaces on the protein surface, generates canonical RNA conformations within a pretrained RNA structural latent space (RiboSphere), and then predicts protein--RNA interaction constraints to bridge the independently defined RNA and protein coordinate frames. The resulting interaction geometry is converted into a geometrically consistent protein-relative pose through rigid placement. We evaluate RiboBridge on a temporally split, sequence-filtered, and redundancy-controlled benchmark of 124 protein--RNA complexes. Under post-hoc interface-correspondence evaluation, where native information is used only after generation to select among already generated predicted-pocket candidates, RiboBridge achieves the highest fNAT and DockQ and the lowest interface and ligand RMSDs among compared methods. Component ablations and stage-wise diagnostics further characterize the contributions of RNA conformational generation, interaction prediction, and rigid placement, identifying the main sources of complex-recovery error.

AI.tldr: RiboBridge is a structure-first framework that separates RNA conformational generation from protein-RNA assembly, achieving state-of-the-art protein-RNA complex prediction on a 124-complex benchmark.
AI.motivation: Designing RNA that binds target proteins requires jointly determining RNA conformation and bound complex geometry without a predefined binding site. Existing methods entangle RNA conformation with protein-relative placement in a unified representation, which couples errors and limits flexibility.
AI.method: RiboBridge first proposes multiple candidate RNA-binding interfaces on the protein surface, generates canonical RNA conformations in a pretrained RNA structural latent space (RiboSphere), predicts protein-RNA interaction constraints to bridge independent RNA and protein coordinate frames, and converts the interaction geometry into a geometrically consistent protein-relative pose via rigid placement.
AI.result: On a temporally split, sequence-filtered, redundancy-controlled benchmark of 124 protein-RNA complexes, under post-hoc interface-correspondence evaluation, RiboBridge achieves the highest fNAT and DockQ and lowest interface/ligand RMSDs versus compared methods. Ablations and stage-wise diagnostics isolate contributions of conformation generation, interaction prediction, and rigid placement.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling RNA conformation from protein-relative assembly via cross-frame interaction geometry is an effective strategy for protein-RNA complex prediction, with diagnostics pinpointing main sources of complex-recovery error.

title: Behavioral Mapping of Hierarchical Dynamical Models Accelerates Bayesian Parameter Inference
summary: Bayesian parameter inference for complex nonlinear dynamical models is often limited by the cost of repeated model simulation. We present a behavioral mapping framework that uses the inferred posterior of a higher-level model to accelerate inference of a lower-level model without requiring state or parameter correspondence between them. Building on approximate simulation relations for hierarchically related models, we define the notion of behavioral compatibility and quantify the behavioral support of detailed model parameters using the reduced model posterior. We learn a level set of behavioral support using a Gaussian process and use it to filter detailed model parameter proposals before expensive simulations during Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) inference. We derive conditions under which the behavioral support level set retains all detailed model parameters that fit the experimental data within a prescribed tolerance. We apply this method to a hierarchy of gene-expression models fitted to cell-free experimental data. After initial setup costs, our approach speeds up MCMC by 8.02% for the phenomenological model and 15.21% for the mechanistic model.

AI.tldr: A behavioral-mapping framework uses the posterior of a coarse/higher-level model to filter parameter proposals for a detailed/lower-level model, accelerating MCMC inference for complex nonlinear dynamical systems without requiring state or parameter correspondence.
AI.motivation: Bayesian parameter inference for complex nonlinear dynamical models is expensive because it requires repeated model simulation. Existing hierarchical or reduced-model approaches typically need correspondence between states or parameters across model levels, which is limiting.
AI.method: Building on approximate simulation relations for hierarchically related models, the authors define behavioral compatibility and quantify the behavioral support of detailed model parameters using the reduced model posterior. They learn a level set of behavioral support with a Gaussian process and use it to filter detailed-model parameter proposals before expensive simulations in MCMC. They derive conditions under which the level set retains all detailed parameters that fit the data within a tolerance.
AI.result: Applied to a hierarchy of gene-expression models fitted to cell-free experimental data, the method (after setup costs) speeds up MCMC by 8.02% for the phenomenological model and 15.21% for the mechanistic model.
AI.conclusion: Posterior information from a reduced higher-level model can be transferred to accelerate inference of a detailed model via learned behavioral support sets, with theoretical guarantees on retaining data-consistent parameters, demonstrating practical speedups in gene-expression inference.

title: Global Convergence of Detailed Balanced Mass Action Systems
comment: 23 pages, 1 figure. Lean 4 formalization: https://github.com/BitMiracle-AI/detailed-balance-gac (tag v1.0). Use of AI tools is described in the Acknowledgements
summary: We give a self-contained proof that, for a finite detailed balanced mass-action system with positive rate constants, each positive stoichiometric compatibility class contains exactly one positive equilibrium and every positive trajectory converges to it, together with a Lean 4 formalization of the complete argument from persistence to convergence. Boundedness and persistence come from the barrier argument of OpenAI (2026) for weakly reversible systems: an arbitrary-tolerance affine approximation yields a finite-minimum barrier whose superlevel sets confine trajectories and give one logarithmic bound for all solutions from a given initial state. The Horn-Jackson dissipation identity identifies the positive equilibria as an exponential family with parameters in the orthogonal complement of the stoichiometric subspace, which gives uniqueness in each class. A bounded-speed descent argument replaces LaSalle's invariance principle; it uses neither uniqueness of solutions nor continuous dependence on initial data, and it places every cluster point in that family. The route given here is direct and elementary, and its main theorem is checked by the Lean kernel against explicit definitions. The proofs, the Lean development, and the manuscript were produced in ClawsGO Science, an agent harness that packages a complete research environment: Claude Opus 5.5 made the research decisions, GPT 6 Astra carried them out, and the Lean kernel checked every formal step.

AI.tldr: A self-contained, elementary proof that finite detailed-balanced mass-action systems have exactly one positive equilibrium per positive stoichiometric compatibility class and that all positive trajectories converge to it, formalized end-to-end in Lean 4.
AI.motivation: The classical result (detailed-balanced systems have unique positive equilibria and global convergence) is usually proved via LaSalle's invariance principle, which requires uniqueness of solutions or continuous dependence on initial data. The authors want a direct, elementary argument for which every step can be machine-checked.
AI.method: Boundedness/persistence via the barrier argument for weakly reversible systems (arbitrary-tolerance affine approximation yielding a finite-minimum barrier with logarithmic bounds); uniqueness of positive equilibria from the Horn-Jackson dissipation identity, viewing equilibria as an exponential family indexed by the orthogonal complement of the stoichiometric subspace; and a bounded-speed descent argument replacing LaSalle that places every cluster point in that family.
AI.result: Each positive stoichiometric compatibility class contains exactly one positive equilibrium, and every positive trajectory converges to it; the full argument from persistence to convergence is checked by the Lean kernel against explicit definitions.
AI.conclusion: The result admits a direct and elementary route avoiding LaSalle's principle, and it is fully formalized. The proofs, Lean development, and manuscript were produced in ClawsGO Science, an agent harness (Claude Opus 5.5 for research decisions, GPT 6 Astra for execution, Lean kernel for verification).
